---

## Recovering missing repository snapshots

Every submission with a GitHub repo field is forked into the EHL snapshot org so
the jury reads a copy under EHL control. When the jury judges **private** repos,
that fork is the only thing they can open: without it they get a 404 on the
team's own repository.

### When this bites

The fork is created by the GitHub bot account. It can fail for reasons that have
nothing to do with the team:

| Cause | Error shape | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub secondary rate limit (fork creation is throttled; a deadline rush of 30+ teams, each retrying, will hit it) | `Could not fork repository (403)` | Wait for the window to clear, then retry |
| Bot token expired | `(401)` | Rotate the token, then retry |
| Token not SSO-authorized for the snapshot org, or missing `repo` scope | `(403)` | Re-authorize in GitHub org settings, then retry |
| Team made the repo private or revoked the bot's access after verifying | `(404)` | Ask the team to re-invite the bot, then retry |

Neither the submit path nor the deadline lock fails the participant when this
happens, by design: the submission is saved either way. The cost of that choice
is that the gap is silent unless an operator looks, which is what this runbook
is for.

### Finding what is missing

`submissions.fork_url IS NULL` is the durable record of a fork still owed.

- **In the admin panel**: `/admin/submissions` shows a **Snapshot** column and, when
  anything is missing, a banner counting them with a per-match retry button.
- **In SQL** (when you want the list outside the UI):

```sql
select t.name as team, s.fields, s.fork_url
from submissions s
join teams t on t.id = s.team_id
join challenges c on c.id = s.challenge_id
where c.chapter_id = '<chapter-id>'
  and s.fork_url is null;
```

### Retrying

1. Fix the underlying cause first (wait out the rate limit, rotate the token, or
   get the bot re-invited). Retrying into the same 403 just burns the limit.
2. Press **Retry N in \<match\>** on `/admin/submissions`, or **Retry snapshot** on a
   single submission's detail page.
3. Read the result. On failure it prints the live GitHub error per team, which
   tells you which of the four causes above you are actually in.
4. Repeat until the banner is gone. The retry is idempotent: a submission that
   already has a fork is skipped without calling GitHub, and an existing fork is
   synced rather than recreated.

### Do this BEFORE judging opens

A juror who cannot open a repo will either score it as broken or stop to ask,
and both cost more than a two-minute check. Confirm the banner on
`/admin/submissions` is clear once the submission deadline has locked and before
jury links go out.

### Preventing it in the first place

- Check the bot token's expiry and scopes before the event (see `docs/PRE-EVENT.md`).
- Encourage teams to submit early and edit later: submission is an upsert, so
  re-submitting updates the row, and early submissions spread fork calls out
/**
 * Snapshot (repo fork) status for a submission.
 *
 * Every submission with a GitHub repo field is forked into the EHL snapshot org
 * so the jury reads a copy under EHL control. Two things can leave that fork
 * missing: a GitHub failure at submit time (secondary rate limit during the
 * deadline rush, an expired bot token, a team revoking access) or the same
 * failure again during the deadline lock.
 *
 * Neither path blocks the participant, by design, so `submissions.fork_url IS
 * NULL` is the ONLY durable record that a fork is owed. This module turns that
 * column into the status admins act on. Keep it dependency-free so it can be
 * used from server components, server actions and unit tests alike.
 */

/** Shown to the team when their submission saved but the fork did not happen. */
export const SNAPSHOT_WARNING =
  "Your submission is saved. We could not archive a copy of your repository yet: organizers will retry automatically. Please keep the repository accessible and do not change its visibility.";

export type SnapshotState = "snapshotted" | "missing" | "not_applicable";

/**
 * Does this submission carry a GitHub repo at all? Mirrors the check the
 * deadline cron already uses, so a submission counted as "missing" here is
 * exactly one the snapshot path would have tried to fork.
 */
export function hasRepoField(fields: Record<string, unknown> | null | undefined): boolean {
  if (!fields) return false;
  return Object.values(fields).some(
    (v) => typeof v === "string" && v.includes("github.com")
  );
}

export function snapshotState(submission: {
  forkUrl: string | null | undefined;
  fields: Record<string, unknown> | null | undefined;
}): SnapshotState {
  if (!hasRepoField(submission.fields)) return "not_applicable";
  return submission.forkUrl ? "snapshotted" : "missing";
}

/**
 * Submissions still owed a fork. This is the retry worklist: an admin runs it
 * once the rate limit window clears or the token is rotated.
 */
export function missingSnapshots<
  T extends { forkUrl: string | null | undefined; fields: Record<string, unknown> | null | undefined }
>(submissions: T[]): T[] {
  return submissions.filter((s) => snapshotState(s) === "missing");
}

    submitProject commits the submission row before forking the team's repo into
    the snapshot org. When GitHub refused the fork, the action returned an error
    after that commit, so the form showed a red failure for a submission that was
    already saved. Teams then retried, spending more of the very secondary rate
    limit that caused the failure in the first place. A deadline rush of private
    repos is exactly when this fires.
    
    The fork is redundant as a gate: the deadline lock re-snapshots every
    submission anyway. So the submit path now keeps the row, returns success, and
    carries a warning explaining the archive copy will be retried.
    
    That trade makes the gap silent, so this also gives operators the means to see
    and close it:
    
    - lockSubmissionsCore collects failedSnapshots alongside failedJuryInvites
      instead of dropping a failed fork on the floor, and wraps each team in its own
      try/catch so one throw no longer abandons every later team.
    - retrySnapshotsCore re-forks submissions with fork_url NULL, scoped to one
      submission or one chapter, reporting the live GitHub error so an admin can
      tell a rate limit from an expired token from revoked access. Idempotent.
    - /admin/submissions gains a Snapshot column, a count of what is missing, and a
      per-match retry button; the detail page gains a per-team retry.
    - The jury pages label a repo link with no EHL fork behind it. They silently
      fell back to the team's own URL, which is a 404 for a juror on a private repo.

    still blocks before the row is written and is unchanged.

    success with a warning; the row is still persisted; gates still block with no
    write), snapshot-retry (records the fork URL, reports the live error, continues
    past a failure, no-ops when nothing is missing), snapshot-status (state
    derivation and the missing-snapshot worklist).

content.text:
It was almost certainly **GitHub's rate limit on creating forks**. The "token" was the GitHub token of our bot account (`ehl-gg`), not an AI token. I'm inferring this from the code and commit history, not from an incident log, so check it against what you remember.

**What happened, in simple terms**

1. When a team submits, the platform makes a copy (a "fork") of their GitHub repo in the `european-hackathon-league` org. That copy is what the jury opens, which matters most for private repos.
2. All the forks are created by one bot account. GitHub only lets one account create so many forks in a short time. This is called a "secondary rate limit".
3. Right before the deadline, 30+ teams submitted within a few minutes. GitHub started refusing forks with `Could not fork repository (403)`.
4. The bug that made it worse: each submission was already saved before the fork step. But when the fork failed, the form still showed teams a red error. They thought their submission had failed and kept retrying. Every retry used up more of the limit, so even more teams were blocked.

**How it was fixed** (commits `0c4cedf`, #114, and `cbafdaa`, #115)
- A failed fork no longer fails the submission. The team sees "Your submission is saved…" with a note that the copy will be retried.
- Missing copies are tracked in the database: a submission whose `submissions.fork_url` is empty still needs one.
- Admins got a retry button.
- Refused submission attempts are now counted and labelled as either "ours" (our side broke) or "theirs" (the team's problem).

**Where to see it**
- **Admin panel → `/admin/submissions`**: the **Snapshot** column shows each submission's copy status. If any are missing, a banner shows the count and a "Retry N in <match>" button. On a single submission's page there's a "Retry snapshot" button, and a failed retry shows GitHub's actual error.
- **Runbook**: `docs/RUNBOOKS.md`, section "Recovering missing repository snapshots". It has a table of possible causes (rate limit, expired token, missing permissions, team made the repo private) and an SQL query that lists affected teams per match.
- **Original errors from the event**: search the Vercel function logs from the deadline window for `Could not fork repository`. Since #115, refused attempts are also written to `event_log`, but events before that fix won't have those entries.

content.text:
The AI code review and the forks both talk to GitHub as the same bot account, so both drew on the same limit. The review got hit in three ways:

**1. The review reads the repo through GitHub's API, not with a clone.**
`lib/code-review/ingest.ts` makes a separate GitHub request for every file it reads, plus a few extra requests per repo. That can mean a few hundred requests for one repo. The workflow runs 10 reviewers in parallel (`.github/workflows/process-code-reviews.yml`), and about 100 repos were reviewed right after the deadline. That is thousands of requests from one account while the teams were still hitting "submit" and creating forks. GitHub allows about 5,000 requests per hour per account, and it also throttles bursts. Once the limit was reached, forks and reviews both got refused.

**2. When the fork was missing, the review went to the team's own repo.**
`app/api/code-review/route.ts:56` uses the EHL fork if there is one, and otherwise the team's original repo. For a private repo the bot often can't open the original, so it gets a 404 and the review fails with `GitHub API error: 404`. So a failed fork caused a failed review later.

**3. Rate-limited files were skipped without any error.**
In `ingest.ts`, when a single file request is refused, the code just skips that file (`if (!contentRes.ok) continue;`). When the limit is reached halfway through a repo, the AI reviews only part of the code, or almost none of it, and the report still looks normal. This is the worst of the three, because nobody sees that anything went wrong.

**Caveat:** in the workflow the token is the `GH_PAT` secret, and in the app it's `GITHUB_TOKEN` (or the admin setting). I can't see secret values, so I'm assuming both are the `ehl-gg` bot token. That fits its scopes (`repo, workflow`), but check it in the repo's secrets settings. If they are different tokens, point 1 gets much weaker. Points 2 and 3 still apply.

**Where to see it**
- **GitHub → `tum-ai/ehl` → Actions → "Process Code Reviews"**: open the runs from the event night. Look for `403`, `rate limit`, or `404` in the job logs.
- **Admin panel, code review status per submission**: reviews marked as failed show the error message.
- **Reviews that "succeeded" but look thin**, with few files and vague comments, are likely cases of point 3.

**Possible fixes:**
- Download each repo as one archive (a single request) instead of one request per file.
- Fail the review, or at least label it, when files were skipped.
- Use a separate token for code review so it doesn't compete with the forks.
- Start reviews only after the fork step has finished.

content.text:
Short version: **GitHub's limit caused only a small part of the failures.** Most failed reviews came from a broken OpenRouter (AI provider) key.

**The real numbers** (production `code_reviews`, read-only query, 82 reviews)

| Match | Completed | Failed | Why they failed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Munich | 45 | 0 | none |
| Paris | 1 | **16** | OpenRouter `401: User not found` on every one |
| Zurich | 16 | **4** | first the AI's answer couldn't be read, then GitHub `403` on the retry |

**Paris (28 June): the AI key was dead**
- All 16 Paris reviews failed on the very first AI call. `User not found` means OpenRouter didn't recognise the API key, for example because it was deleted or belonged to a removed account. GitHub played no part here: every Paris repo already had its EHL copy.
- Someone updated the `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` secret in GitHub at 11:09:17 and re-ran everything 8 seconds later. It failed the same way, 17 out of 17.
- Probable reason: the worker reads the key from **admin settings in the database first**, and uses the GitHub secret only if that's empty (`lib/code-review/openrouter.ts:34`). An old key saved there would override the new secret. The database key was only replaced on 22 Aug at 21:28, and the one Paris review that succeeded ran two minutes later (21:30). I can't see what the database held on 28 June, so this is likely but not proven.
- **The other 15 Paris reviews were never re-run.** They are still marked failed today.

**Zurich (13 Sept): two problems, one after the other**
1. **At 10:21–10:27, 6 reviews failed with errors like `Unterminated string in JSON`.** The final "coordinator" AI step returned broken JSON, most likely because its answer was cut off at its 3,000-token length limit. That may be the "token limit" people remember. The code has no safety net for this step (`lib/code-review/pipeline.ts`, the `coordParsed = parseJson(...)` line), so one bad answer fails the whole review. The earlier sub-reviews had already run successfully and were paid for.
2. **At 10:31, those were re-queued, and 4 of them now failed with `GitHub API error: 403` in under a second.** Ten minutes earlier the same repos had downloaded fine. GitHub refusing the very first request means the bot's GitHub request limit was used up, after 16 reviews that each downloaded file by file on top of the deadline activity. That's the rate-limit problem I described before, but it only hit these retries. 2 of the 6 recovered on the retry. The other 4 are still failed.

**Correction to what I said earlier:** I guessed that reviews might have quietly skipped files. The data doesn't show that. The completed reviews stopped at the intended ~50k-token budget (`sampled: true`), which is the normal cap, not a GitHub refusal.

**Where to see this yourself**
- **Error per team:** admin panel → code reviews (the message is stored in `code_reviews.progress`).
- **Full logs:** GitHub → `tum-ai/ehl` → Actions → "Process Code Reviews". Paris is runs `28319973538` and `28320262313` (28 June). Zurich is `34751640924`, `34751804432` (JSON errors) and `34752073942`, `34752109371` (403s) on 13 Sept.

**What I'd do next**
1. Re-queue the 19 still-failed reviews (15 Paris, 4 Zurich). The current key works: I tested it and got a 200. Re-queuing starts paid AI runs, so I'll only do it if you say so.
2. Code fixes:
   - Retry the coordinator step once when its JSON is broken, and give it a higher token limit.
   - Show admins which key is actually in use: database or GitHub secret.
   - Download each repo in one request instead of file by file.

Okay, now don't only approximate, but really look into how many submissions are possible with the token we currently have. What kind of token is that? If one team submits one time and there is one fork per team, how many teams can we do in what space of time? Research the GitHub token for that, the exact rate limits, and, based on the history, say if and what kind of limit we were hitting, because I want a real, backed, deep dive and analysis of that.
I'll dig into this in four parts: what the token is, how many GitHub calls each submission makes, GitHub's official limits, and what actually happened at the deadline.

-- Event Log: Append-only audit trail with hash-chain integrity.
-- All critical mutations are logged here. Supports forensic investigation
-- and financial compliance for prize money distribution (15k€).
--
-- Design: Transaction-based logging (like a bank ledger).
-- Deltas are logged, not full state. State recovery comes from DB backups.
-- Hash-chain makes tampering detectable.

CREATE TABLE event_log (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  -- What happened
  action TEXT NOT NULL,              -- e.g. 'application.submitted', 'score.published'
  entity_type TEXT NOT NULL,         -- e.g. 'application', 'team', 'chapter', 'score'
  entity_id TEXT NOT NULL,           -- UUID or identifier of affected entity
  -- Who did it
  actor_id UUID REFERENCES profiles(id),  -- NULL for system actions (cron, automated)
  actor_type TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'admin', -- 'admin', 'participant', 'jury', 'system'
  -- What changed (delta, not full state)
  delta JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  -- Integrity: hash-chain for tamper detection
  prev_hash TEXT,                    -- entry_hash of the previous log entry
  entry_hash TEXT NOT NULL,          -- SHA-256 of (action + entity + delta + prev_hash + created_at)
  -- Context
  metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}',       -- IP, batch_id, snapshot (for critical locks)
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Performance indexes
CREATE INDEX idx_event_log_entity ON event_log(entity_type, entity_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_event_log_action ON event_log(action);

Token issuance for Actions workflows was also affected, impacting approximately 4% of workflows during the incident time frame. Creating issues through the web interface failed for about 96% of attempts, and signup failures were above 90%.

The cause was an internal data-cleanup job that began writing to a shared database cluster at 07:33 UTC. That cluster stores permission data read on nearly every authenticated request. The safeguard that was pacing the background job watched only one health signal — how far the database replicas were lagging — and that signal stayed low the whole time. It did not account for the load building on the primary itself, so the job kept writing while the primary quietly ran toward its limit.

When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that needed it could not complete. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast, and the shared request-handling capacity degraded into site-wide errors. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept re-sending the writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover.

Monitoring declared the incident at 08:50 UTC, but due to the broad impact and amplification from token creation, it took time to identify the source of the load. First responders mitigated by shedding internal load and pausing the job, and all services recovered by 10:44 UTC.

To prevent recurrence, we are rate-limiting background jobs against shared, customer-serving databases by default, and adding automatic pausing and paging on primary-server load rather than replication lag alone. We are also surfacing running background work directly alongside database health signals so responders can see and pause it without leaving those dashboards, bounding retries in the token-issuing path, and adding request-level timeouts so one unhealthy database cannot consume shared web server capacity. name: github-token-capacity-analysis
description: Findings (2026-09-29) on the ehl-gg GitHub token, its rate limits, and why Zurich forks/reviews failed on 2026-09-13

Deep dive done 2026-09-29 against production data + GitHub API.

- Token: classic PAT (ghp_) of user `ehl-gg`, scopes delete_repo/repo/workflow, no expiry. 5,000 req/h core. Snapshot org `european-hackathon-league` is on the Free plan, so the org audit log is UI-only (no API).

- Zurich (2026-09-13): GitHub had a critical incident 08:43-10:44 UTC (auth/permission DB saturated). Fork failures (ERK 09:02 with no load; all attempts 09:56:56-09:57:40) fall inside it.
- Zurich deadline lock never finished on its own: it measured ~33-40s per team (it copies up to 100 Entire refs per team, 3 calls each, plus jury invites) against a 300s maxDuration and 600s lease. An admin set "pitching" by hand at 10:24:40, so most jury invites were never sent.
- Code-review ingest bug: after the char budget fills, it keeps downloading every remaining file and discards it. Replay: ~4,600 GitHub calls for 19 Zurich repos (median 198, max 727).
- Vercel runtime logs only reach back ~1 day, so the raw GitHub error bodies from event days are lost. That is why [[password-reset-safelinks-fix]]-style durable logging matters.

**Why:** the docs/RUNBOOKS.md claim "a deadline rush of 30+ teams will hit the secondary rate limit" is unverified; Munich disproved it.
**How to apply:** when revisiting snapshot/lock/code-review GitHub load, start from these measurements and don't re-derive them. Recommend persisting GitHub error bodies and x-ratelimit headers durably.

content.text:
Short answer: **we mostly didn't hit a GitHub limit, and teams were never blocked from submitting.** Paris and Munich had zero fork failures; Munich did 43 forks in about an hour without a problem. The Zurich failures happened during a **GitHub outage**, and our own deadline code made them worse. The runbook's claim that "30+ teams will hit the rate limit" is contradicted by Munich.

## 1. The token

| | |
|---|---|
| Type | **Classic personal access token** (`ghp_…`) |
| Account | `ehl-gg`, a normal user account, admin of `european-hackathon-league` |
| Scopes | `repo`, `workflow`, `delete_repo` |
| Expiry | none set |
| Used by | the Vercel app (verify, submit, deadline lock, retry) |

I checked this with GitHub's API, which doesn't use up quota. One gap: the AI review workflow uses a separate secret, `GH_PAT`. I can't see which account it belongs to (the snapshot org has three members: `ehl-gg`, you, and `s1k0ra`). If it's also `ehl-gg`, everything shares one allowance.

## 2. GitHub's limits for this token

From GitHub's docs (rate limits page):

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Requests per hour | **5,000** (the page lists 15,000 only for apps on the paid Enterprise Cloud plan) |
| Burst "points" per minute | **900** (a read costs 1 point, a write costs 5) |
| Writes that create content | **80 per minute, 500 per hour** |
| Requests at the same time | 100 |

When you go over, GitHub returns a 403 or 429. For the hourly limit, the response header `x-ratelimit-remaining` is `0`. For a burst limit, the error message says "secondary rate limit". That message is the only way to tell which limit was hit, and we don't have it from the event (see section 5).

## 3. What one team costs (from the code, and measured where possible)

- **Minimal team** (no session-history refs, no jury invites, one submit, deadline lock): about **12 requests, 3 of them writes**.
- **Zurich-like team**: about **216 requests, 127 of them writes**. The difference comes from two features:
  - **Copying session-history refs.** At submit and again at the deadline, the code copies up to 100 of the team's Entire checkpoint refs into the fork, costing 2–3 requests per ref. I measured the real forks: Zurich averaged about 38 refs per team, and 5 teams hit the 100 cap.
  - **Jury invites.** 9 jurors × 20 forks.
- **AI code review, per repo**: I replayed the review code against the 19 real Zurich repos I could read. It took **4,569 GitHub calls, median 198 and max 727 per repo**. Much of that is a bug: once the reading budget is nearly full, it keeps downloading every remaining file only to throw it away.

## 4. Capacity: how many teams, in what time

| Scenario | Hourly limit (5,000) | Burst limit (900 pts/min) | Writes (500/h) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal team, no review | ~400 teams/h | ~37 teams/min | **~160 teams/h** ← binding |
| Minimal team + AI review on same token | **~23 teams/h** ← binding | | |
| Zurich-like team, no review | ~23 teams/h | **~1 team/min** | ~4 teams/h, in theory* |
| Zurich-like team + AI review | **~12 teams/h** | | |

\* GitHub doesn't document which endpoints count as "content-creating". Munich created about 2,900 refs in its forks with no fork ever failing, so in practice ref copies don't seem to be held to the 500/h cap.

There's also a limit of our own that is lower than any of GitHub's. **The deadline lock can only process about 8 teams per run.** I measured its speed on Zurich day from the jury-invite timestamps: about 33–40 seconds per team. That was during GitHub's outage, so it may be faster on a normal day. A run is killed after 300 seconds, and a killed run blocks the next one for up to 10 minutes. With 20 Zurich-like teams, it can't finish.

## 5. What actually happened, per event

**Paris (28 June):** all 17 forks were created within 1 second of submitting, and the lock finished in one tick. The failed reviews were the OpenRouter key problem, unrelated to GitHub.

**Munich (23 Aug):** 43 forks, every one within about 1 second of submitting, including 20 teams in the last 10 minutes. The lock finished in one tick. **No GitHub limit was hit.**

**Zurich (13 Sept):**
- GitHub had a **critical incident from 08:43 to 10:44 UTC**. According to GitHub's status page, the database that checks permissions on almost every logged-in request ran out of connections. That window covers the whole Zurich deadline.
- **Fork failures during the outage:**
  - ERK failed at 09:02, when nothing else was running.
  - Every fork attempt between 09:56:56 and 09:57:40 failed, public and private repos alike (5 teams).
  - Everything before and after that window worked.

  That points to GitHub's side, not our traffic.
- **The deadline lock** started at about 10:00 and never finished on its own. Each fork's description tells me which path created it: Beta, y/agent and TimeLapse were created by the lock, and AskOnce by the admin retry button. An admin had to set "pitching" by hand at 10:24:40. As a side effect, **most jury invites were never sent**: 5 forks have no juror at all, and the rest have 1–2 of the 7.
- **The review 403s at 10:31** came during the outage and after a very heavy hour: the lock runs plus about 4,600 review calls, if `GH_PAT` is the same token. That is the one point where the hourly limit may really have been hit. I can't prove it without the response headers.

## 6. What I can't prove, and why

- Vercel only keeps function logs for about 1 day. My requests for 13 Sept return errors, so the exact GitHub error texts are gone.
- The snapshot org is on GitHub's Free plan, which has no audit-log API. As an org owner, you can still browse it at `github.com/organizations/european-hackathon-league/settings/audit-log`.
- Next time, the fix is to save GitHub's error text and `x-ratelimit-*` headers in `event_log`.

## 7. What would actually raise capacity

1. **Make the lock resumable**: process a batch of teams per cron tick and skip teams that are already done, instead of redoing all 20 every run. This is our real ceiling.
2. **Copy refs only when they changed**: stop re-copying up to 100 refs on every resubmit and lock pass.
3. **Fix the review bug** so it stops downloading after the budget is full, and give code review its own token.
4. Record GitHub's error text and headers durably (see section 6).
5. **Correct the runbook's rate-limit claim.**

I saved these findings to memory. I can also put this into a shareable page for the team, or start on fixes 1–3.

You said Munich didn't have any problems. That's not true. I had submitted two teams manually, the same as Zurich. Now, looking at point 4 of your capacity table, I understand that copying the refs is eating up a lot of things. I thought we were just cloning the repository with all the branches. Why do we copy them, and why does it take up so much of the limit?

You're right about Munich, and I'm sorry: I saw those two teams in the data and then left them out of my conclusion. Two teams, **alpha** (10:39) and **Tetrad** (10:43), were submitted after the deadline, and both still have **no fork**. So Munich did have a problem. The 43 teams that submitted through the normal form got their forks, but that doesn't mean the event went smoothly. The data doesn't tell me why those two needed manual submission. If you remember what they ran into, I can check it against the code.

## Why we copy refs at all

The fork **does not** clone the whole repository with all branches. Two things are going on:

1. **We fork only the main branch.** The fork call passes `default_branch_only: true` (`lib/github.ts:147`), so other branches never reach the EHL copy.
2. **Entire's session history isn't stored on a branch.** Entire keeps each coding session as a separate "ref" (a named pointer to a commit) under `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, one per checkpoint. Forking only carries over branches (and tags when all branches are forked). Custom refs like these are left behind, so even a full fork with every branch would not include the session history.

So after the fork, the code copies those refs into the fork one by one (`fetchCheckpointBranchIntoFork`, `lib/github.ts:204`). The comment there explains why: it keeps the session record under EHL control, so a team can't delete it after the deadline, and the jury and AI review can read it.

## Why it uses so much of the limit

The data itself costs nothing. A fork shares its storage with the original repo, so GitHub copies no files, only small pointers. The expensive part is **how** the pointers are created:

- **GitHub has no "copy many refs at once" call.** Each ref needs:
  - 1 read to look up which commit it points to,
  - 1 write to create it in the fork,
  - and if it already exists, a failed write plus 1 more write to update it.
  
  That's 2–3 requests per ref, and writes count 5× toward the per-minute budget.
- **Up to 100 refs per team:** that's 200–300 requests for a single team.
- **It starts from zero every time.** Every resubmit, every deadline-lock pass and every retry re-copies all of them, without checking what's already in the fork. That's why Zurich forks now hold hundreds of refs, and some have more than 500.
- **The per-ref lookup is wasted.** The call that lists the refs already returns which commit each one points to, so about a third of these requests could be skipped.
- **It runs even where it isn't needed.** The copy runs on every submission, whether or not the challenge requires Entire. Zurich's two challenges had `entire_required: false`, yet they still paid the full cost.

## Cheaper options, from least to most change

1. **Reuse the commit info from the list call** instead of looking up each ref again. This saves about ⅓ of the requests with a tiny change.
2. **Copy only refs that are new or changed.** List the fork's refs once and skip any that already match. Resubmits and lock passes would drop from hundreds of requests per team to a handful.
3. **Only copy when the challenge actually uses Entire.**
4. **Copy with one git push instead of the REST API.** A single `git fetch`/`git push` of `refs/entire/*` moves every ref in one operation and doesn't count against the 5,000-per-hour allowance. Vercel functions don't include git, though, so this would have to run somewhere like GitHub Actions.

Options 1–3 are small code changes and remove most of the load. Should I implement them?
i like option 4. but does that guarantee that for example 100 teams can submit all at once?

No. Option 4 removes the biggest cost, but it doesn't make 100 teams submitting at once safe. Here's what still stands in the way.

## What's left after option 4

Each team still needs a few GitHub API calls that git can't replace:

| Step | Requests | Of which writes |
|---|---|---|
| Verify repo | 1–4 | 0–1 (accepting the bot invite) |
| Create fork | 2 | 2 (fork + description) |
| Trigger the git copy job | 1 | 1 |
| **Per team** | **~5–7** | **~3–4** |

For **100 teams in the same minute**, compared with GitHub's documented burst limits:

- **Writes:** about 300–400. The limit for writes that create content is **80 per minute**. Creating a fork is clearly such a write. **Over the limit.**
- **Burst points:** about 1,700. The limit is **900 per minute**. **Over the limit.**
- **Hourly total:** about 700 of 5,000. **Fine.**

So even with option 4, 100 teams in one minute would hit the burst limit. Spread over **3–5 minutes**, the same 100 teams fit.

## Other limits option 4 adds or leaves in place

- **Git itself has limits.** GitHub doesn't publish numbers for them, but a burst of 100 pushes from one account can still be slowed down or refused.
- **GitHub Actions has a cap on jobs running at once**: about 20 on the free plan. 100 separate jobs would queue, and each takes 20–60 seconds just to start. One job that processes every pending team in turn works much better than one job per team.
- **Other limits stay as they are:**
  - The deadline lock can still only handle about 8 teams per run.
  - Jury invites still cost 1 write per juror per fork.
  - The AI review still downloads about 200 files per repo.
- **GitHub outages.** No design prevents what happened in Zurich. You can only design so an outage doesn't hurt anyone.

## What would guarantee it: stop doing GitHub work at submit time

The only real guarantee is to take GitHub out of the moment of submitting:

1. **Submitting only saves to our database.** No GitHub call happens at submit, so 100 teams, or 1,000, get "submitted" instantly. That part depends only on Supabase and Vercel.
2. **A queue does the GitHub work afterwards, at a controlled pace**, for example 15–20 forks per minute. That stays under the 80 writes/minute limit with room to spare.
3. **The queue retries automatically.** When GitHub says "slow down" (including its wait time) or is down, the queue waits and tries again instead of failing. A Zurich-style outage would then only delay forks, not lose them.
4. **Option 4 runs inside that queue**: one Actions job copies every team's session history with git.
5. **The deadline lock just checks the queue is empty** and no longer redoes every team.

With that design, 100 teams submitting in the same minute would have all their forks within about 5–7 minutes, and nobody would see an error. The trade-off is that the jury gets repos a few minutes after the deadline instead of instantly. In practice that was already the case.

To prove it before the next event, we'd run the queue against 100 test repos with a **separate test bot account**. Testing on `ehl-gg` could get the production bot throttled.

Should I write this up as a plan: queue, rate-limited worker, git copy in Actions, and the lock change?

# Handoff: GitHub rate limits, repo snapshots and code-review failures

Local working note, **not for commit** (this repo is public and the note names
teams, repos and internal settings). Written 2026-09-29 from a read-only
investigation of production data, the GitHub API, GitHub Actions logs and the
code on branch `feat/apply-creates-account` (commit `bf28432`).

Every number below was observed directly unless it is marked **(model)**.
Model numbers are derived from the code paths and should be confirmed by
measurement before anyone relies on them.

---

## 1. TL;DR

1. The bot token is a **classic PAT of the user `ehl-gg`**: 5,000 REST
   requests/hour, plus GitHub's burst limits (80 content-creating writes/min,
   500/hour, 900 points/min).
2. **Paris (2026-06-28):** GitHub was not the problem. All 17 forks were
   created within 1 s of submission. **16 of 17 AI reviews failed on a dead
   OpenRouter key** (`401 User not found`).
3. **Munich (2026-08-23):** 43 teams submitted normally and every fork was
   created within about 2 s. **Two teams (`alpha`, `Tetrad`) had to be
   submitted manually after the deadline and still have no fork** (`fork_url`
   NULL). Why they needed manual submission is **unknown**; the operator
   confirms it happened.
4. **Zurich (2026-09-13):**
   - GitHub had a **critical incident from 08:43 to 10:44 UTC**. It covers the
     whole deadline window, and all fork failures fall inside it.
   - Our **deadline lock never finished on its own**. It measured about
     33 to 40 s per team, against a 300 s function limit and a 600 s lease. An
     admin forced "pitching" at 10:24:40.
   - As a result, **most jury invites were never sent**.
   - The AI reviews then hit **GitHub 403** at 10:31. That may be the hourly
     limit being used up, the outage, or both; it cannot be proven now.
5. **The main GitHub cost in our code is copying Entire checkpoint refs**:
   - up to 100 refs per team,
   - 2 to 3 REST calls per ref, one ref at a time,
   - redone from scratch on every resubmit, lock pass and retry,
   - and run **even when the challenge does not require Entire**.
6. **The second cost is AI-review ingest**: about 200 GitHub calls per repo
   (median), 727 at most. Part of that is a bug: after the budget is full it
   keeps downloading files and throws them away.
7. The runbook claim "a deadline rush of 30+ teams will hit the secondary
   rate limit" (`docs/RUNBOOKS.md`, "Recovering missing repository
   snapshots") is **contradicted by Munich**: 43 forks at a deadline rush with
   zero failures.
8. **No design can guarantee 100 simultaneous submissions at submit time**,
   because fork creation alone exceeds the 80 writes/minute limit. The
   guarantee comes from taking GitHub out of the submit path: save to the DB,
   then fork from a rate-limited, retrying queue (section 8).

---

## 2. The token

Checked 2026-09-29 with `GET /user` and `GET /rate_limit` (neither call uses
up quota), using `GITHUB_TOKEN` from `.env.local`.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Type | Classic personal access token (`ghp_` prefix, 40 chars) |
| Account | `ehl-gg`, `type: User`, created 2026-04-25 |
| Scopes (`x-oauth-scopes`) | `delete_repo, repo, workflow` |
| Expiry | none (no `github-authentication-token-expiration` header) |
| Core limit | 5,000/hour (`x-ratelimit-limit: 5000`) |
| Search limit | 30/min (used by the jury email fallback in `addCollaborators`) |
| Role in snapshot org | `admin` of `european-hackathon-league` |
| Snapshot org plan | **Free**: no audit-log API. The web UI still works for owners at `github.com/organizations/european-hackathon-league/settings/audit-log` |
| Snapshot org members | `ehl-gg`, `mykhayloserdyuk`, `s1k0ra` (+4 outside collaborators) |
| `app_settings.github_token` | **not set**, so the app uses the env var |

**Caveats:**
- I compared `.env.local` only. I did not compare it with the Vercel
  production value.
- The review workflow uses a **different secret, `GH_PAT`**
  (`.github/workflows/process-code-reviews.yml`, `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GH_PAT }}`,
  last updated 2026-04-29). Its owner is **unverified**. It must be one of
  the three org members, since it reads the private forks. If it is `ehl-gg`,
  the review and the app share one 5,000/hour budget.

---

## 3. GitHub's documented limits

Source: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api
(fetched 2026-09-29)

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Primary, PAT / authenticated user | **5,000 requests/hour** |
| Primary, GitHub App on Enterprise Cloud | 15,000/hour |
| Concurrent requests | max **100** |
| REST points | max **900 points/min**. GET/HEAD/OPTIONS = 1 point, POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE = 5 points |
| CPU time | 90 s of CPU per 60 s of real time |
| Content-generating requests | max **80/min** and **500/hour** |

**How to tell the two limits apart** (also from the docs):
- **Primary limit hit:** 403 or 429 with `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0`.
- **Secondary limit hit:** 403 or 429 with an error message saying a
  secondary rate limit was exceeded.
- We never stored either, so we cannot tell afterwards (section 7).

**Forks** (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/forks):
- Forking is asynchronous.
- It returns 202, or 422 if "the endpoint has been spammed".
- No fork-specific numeric limit is documented.
- The docs do **not** list which endpoints count as "content-generating".
  Empirically (Munich, section 5.2), creating git refs did not block forks,
  even though thousands of refs were created.

---

## 4. Code map: every GitHub call per team

### 4.1 Call sites

| Path | File | GitHub calls |
|---|---|---|
| Verify button | `app/api/submissions/verify-repo/route.ts` | GET repo. On a private repo: GET `user/repository_invitations` + PATCH accept + GET repo again. GET `collaborators/ehl-gg`. If `entire_required`: `checkCheckpointBranch` (below) |
| Submit | `lib/actions/submissions.ts` ~L325-444 | If `entire_required`: `checkCheckpointBranch`. Then `snapshotRepo` (L425), then **`fetchCheckpointBranchIntoFork` (L441), called unconditionally** |
| `snapshotRepo` | `lib/github.ts:105` | GET fork. If it exists: POST `merge-upstream`. Else: POST `/forks` with `default_branch_only: true` (L147) + PATCH description |
| `fetchCheckpointBranchIntoFork` | `lib/github.ts:204` | `listEntireCheckpointRefs` (GET matching-refs, 100/page, capped at `MAX_ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_REFS = 100`, `lib/entire.ts:51`). Then **for each ref, one at a time**: GET source ref + POST create. On 422 (exists): PATCH. Plus 2 legacy candidate GETs |
| Deadline lock | `lib/submissions-lock.ts` ~L109-180 (`lockSubmissionsCore`) | For each submission, one at a time: `snapshotRepo` + `fetchCheckpointBranchIntoFork` + `addCollaborators` if `invite_jury_to_forks` (one PUT per juror, search API if no username) |
| Retry | `lib/submissions-lock.ts` ~L206-300 (`retrySnapshotsCore`) | same snapshot + copy, description `EHL submission snapshot (retry): …` |
| Cron | `app/api/cron/deadline-check/route.ts` | `vercel.json` runs it **every minute**. `maxDuration = 300` (L13), lease `LOCK_TTL_SECONDS = 600` (L23). Calls `lockSubmissionsCore` for every challenge, and only **after** all of them sets the chapter to `pitching`. A run killed at 300 s never releases its lease, so the next run cannot start for up to 10 min |
| AI review | `scripts/process-code-reviews.ts` → `lib/code-review/ingest.ts` | GET repo, tree, commits, then **one GET per file** (`/contents/`). 10 parallel workers (workflow matrix) |

### 4.2 Why refs are copied at all

- Entire stores each coding session as a separate ref under
  `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>` (plus legacy
  `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` and `refs/entire/checkpoints/v1.1`).
- A GitHub fork copies branches only. Here it copies **only the default
  branch** (`default_branch_only: true`).
- Custom refs are never copied, even by a full fork.
- The comment at `lib/github.ts:187-203` says the copy exists to keep the
  session record under EHL control.
- The git objects themselves are free, because a fork shares its object
  store with the original. **The cost is only the REST call per ref.**

### 4.3 Waste in the ref copy

- The matching-refs list response **already contains each ref's SHA**, yet
  the code does one more GET per ref to fetch it.
- The code never lists the fork's existing refs, so every pass re-POSTs all
  of them. Each POST fails with 422 and is followed by a PATCH.
- The copy runs regardless of the `entire_required` setting. Zurich's two
  challenges had `entire_required: false` and still paid it.

### 4.4 AI-review ingest bug

Location: `lib/code-review/ingest.ts`, the download loop after the
`relevantItems.sort(...)` call.

- Files are sorted priority-first, then by size **ascending**, so the review
  makes many small requests.
- When a file would overflow `charBudget`, the loop sets `sampled = true` and
  `continue`s. For non-priority files it does not `break`.
- `totalChars` stops growing, so the loop's `totalChars >= charBudget` exit
  check **never triggers**. **Every remaining relevant file is downloaded and
  thrown away.**
- Evidence: see the replay in section 5.4. ERK cost 727 calls for 288 files
  used.

- `lib/code-review/openrouter.ts:34`: the OpenRouter key comes from
  `app_settings.openrouter_api_key` **before** the env/Actions secret. A stale
  DB key silently overrides a rotated secret.
- `lib/code-review/pipeline.ts`: the coordinator's `parseJson(coordResult.content)`
  is **not wrapped in try/catch**, while the tech-description parse is. One

- `app/api/code-review/route.ts:56` and `scripts/process-code-reviews.ts`

## 6. Capacity model (per `ehl-gg` token, current code)

**(model)** Per-team request counts come from the call sites in section 4.
N = checkpoint refs copied (Zurich average ≈ 38), J = jurors invited.

| Step | Minimal team (N=0, J=0, public) | Zurich-like team (N≈38, J=9, private) |
|---|---|---|
| Verify | 1 GET | ~3 GET + 1 write |
| First submit | 1 GET + 2 writes (fork, description) + 3 GET (list, 2 legacy) | N+4 GET + N+2 writes ≈ 42 GET + 40 writes |
| Deadline lock | 4 GET + 1 write (merge-upstream) | N+6 GET + (2N+1) + J writes ≈ 44 GET + 86 writes |
| **Total** | **~9 GET + 3 writes = 12 req, 24 points** | **~89 GET + 127 writes = 216 req, ~724 points** |
| Each extra resubmit | +4 GET + 1 write | +N+4 GET + 2N+1 writes (≈ +42 GET + 77 writes) |
| AI review (same token?) | +~198 GET (median) | +~198 GET |

**(model)** Throughput limits:

| Scenario | 5,000/hour | 900 points/min | 80 writes/min, 500/hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal, no review | ~400 teams/h | ~37 teams/min | 26/min, **~160 teams/h (binding)** |
| Minimal + review on same token | **~23 teams/h (binding)** | | |
| Zurich-like, no review | ~23 teams/h | **~1 team/min (binding)** | ~4 teams/h *if* ref writes count; Munich suggests they are not enforced |
| Zurich-like + review | **~12 teams/h** | | |
| **Our own lock** | **~8 teams per 300 s run** (measured, section 5.3), then up to 10 min blocked | | |

**100 teams in one minute, even with the ref copy removed:**
- about 300-400 writes against the 80/min limit, and about 1,700 points
  against 900/min.
- **Not possible in one minute. Spread over 3-5 minutes, it fits.**

---

## 7. What cannot be proven, and why

- **Vercel runtime logs** reach back only about 1 day. `vercel logs --since`
  with any start date older than a day returns `Response Error (400)`. The
  `Could not fork repository (<status>): <body>` lines from event days are
  gone. So is `failedSnapshots` from the lock.
- The **org audit log** has no API on the Free plan. The UI may show
  `repo.create` / fork events, but not failed attempts.
- **Why Munich's alpha/Tetrad** needed manual submission: not recorded
  anywhere I could read.
- **Whether `GH_PAT` is `ehl-gg`.**
- **Whether git-ref POSTs count** toward the 80/min and 500/hour limits.
- **Primary vs secondary limit vs outage for the Zurich 403s**: headers and
  bodies were never stored.

---

## 8. Recommended actions

Ordered by value. Each action lists the evidence behind it. Per `CLAUDE.md`,
every code change needs tests (bugfix: failing test first) and must pass
`pnpm typecheck && pnpm test && pnpm build`, plus E2E.

### A. Make failures durable and diagnosable (do first, small)

- Log every non-2xx GitHub response to `event_log`: endpoint, status,
  message body, `x-ratelimit-remaining`, `x-ratelimit-resource`,
  `retry-after`.
- Write one row per failed snapshot or ref copy, and per lock-run
  start/finish.
- Evidence: section 7. Every root-cause question above stays open only
  because this was missing.

### B. Take GitHub out of the submit path: queue + rate-limited worker

This is what "100 teams at once" needs.

- Submit writes the row plus a "snapshot pending" marker. **No GitHub call at
  submit.**
  - `submissions.fork_url IS NULL` is already the durable "fork owed" signal
    (`lib/snapshot-status.ts`).
  - Consider an explicit state column so failures and backoff are
    visible.
- A worker processes pending snapshots at a fixed pace (about 15-20 forks/min,
  well under 80 writes/min):
  - honor `retry-after` / `x-ratelimit-reset`;
  - use exponential backoff on 5xx/403;
  - make it idempotent (already true for `snapshotRepo`).
- Candidate runtimes:
  - the existing every-minute cron with a **bounded batch per tick** that
    finishes well under `maxDuration`;
  - or one GitHub Actions job. Actions allows about 20 concurrent jobs on
    the free plan, so use **one job processing the queue**, not one job per
    team.
- Evidence:
  - fork creation alone is ~3 writes per team, so 100 teams = 300 writes,
    more than the 80/min limit (section 6);
  - Zurich's outage failures would become delays, not losses.
- To test: a **separate test bot account** and a test org with about 100
  test repos. Do not load-test on `ehl-gg`.

### C. Fix the deadline lock so it always finishes

- Process in bounded, resumable batches: skip submissions whose fork and ref
  copy are already current.
- Set `pitching` independently of GitHub work finishing. Locking is a DB
  operation; snapshots can continue afterwards via the queue.
- Stop re-copying refs on every pass.
- Evidence:
  - measured about 33-40 s per team: 300 s gives about 8 teams;
  - Zurich needed a manual `pitching` at 10:24:40;
  - most jury invites were never sent (section 5.3).

### D. Cut the ref-copy cost

In order of effort:

1. Use the SHA already in the `matching-refs` response. This drops 1 GET
   per ref, about ⅓ of the calls.
2. List the fork's refs once and copy **only new or changed** refs. That
   drops the 422 + PATCH per existing ref, which dominate resubmits and lock
   passes.
3. Copy only when the challenge needs Entire (`entire_required`, or if the
   session analysis is needed anyway, make that an explicit setting).
   Zurich had `entire_required: false` and still copied about 770 refs per
   pass.
4. **Operator's preferred direction: copy via git, not REST.**
   - One `git fetch <source> 'refs/entire/*:refs/entire/*'` followed by
     `git push <fork> 'refs/entire/*:refs/entire/*'` moves every ref in one
     operation, outside the REST 5,000/hour budget.
   - Needs a git binary, so not in Vercel functions. Run it in the queue
     worker (GitHub Actions).
   - Git operations have their own **undocumented** limits: batch and pace
     them too.
   - Mind the Entire checkpoint cap semantics (`MAX_ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_REFS`).
     A git push has no 100 cap. Decide whether that is wanted: it would also
     copy much more.

### E. Fix the AI-review ingest

- `break` out of the download loop once the budget is reached. Only
  priority files may still be fetched.
- Better: fetch the repo as **one tarball/zipball** (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball`,
  1 call) instead of one call per file.
- Give code review **its own token**, and confirm who owns `GH_PAT`.
- Evidence: section 5.4. 4,569 calls for 19 repos, median 198, max 727.

### F. Review-pipeline robustness (not GitHub, found on the way)

- Wrap the coordinator `parseJson` in try/catch with one retry. Consider
  raising `max_tokens` above 3,000. Evidence: 6 Zurich failures of this kind.
- Make the OpenRouter key source visible to admins, or prefer the secret.
  Evidence: Paris 401s continued after the secret rotation (section 5.1).

### G. Docs

- Correct `docs/RUNBOOKS.md`, "Recovering missing repository snapshots".
  The "30+ teams will hit the secondary rate limit" claim is unverified and
  contradicted by Munich.
- Add the outage case, the lock-timeout case, and how to read the new
  event_log rows from A.

---

## 9. Pending operational items

All of these need operator approval: they are paid, outward-facing, or both.

- **Re-run the 19 still-failed AI reviews**: 15 Paris + 4 Zurich. The
  OpenRouter key currently validates (`GET /api/v1/key` → 200, checked
  2026-09-29). This triggers paid LLM runs.
- **Create forks for Munich `alpha` and `Tetrad`** (`fork_url` NULL). Use
  the admin retry on `/admin/submissions`.
- **Send the missing Zurich jury invites** if the jury still needs access.
  5 forks have none, the rest are partial.
- Confirm the **owner of `GH_PAT`**.
- Ask the operator **why Munich alpha/Tetrad** were submitted manually.

---

## 10. Reproducing the data (all read-only)

- **Supabase:** REST with `apikey` + `Authorization: Bearer <SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY>`
  from `.env.local`. Tables and selects used:
  - `code_reviews?select=id,status,progress,repo_url,queued_at,generated_at,repo_metadata,submission:submissions(fork_url,fields,challenge:challenges(title,chapter:chapters(name)))`.
    `progress` holds the failure message.
  - `submissions?select=id,submitted_at,updated_at,fork_url,fields,team:teams(name),challenge:challenges(title,chapter:chapters(name,submission_deadline,status))`.
  - `event_log?select=action,actor_type,delta,created_at,entity_id&or=(action.like.submission*,action.eq.chapter.status_changed,action.eq.chapter.updated)`.
    For `submission.*`, `entity_id` is the **challenge** id. There are no
    `submission.blocked` rows yet.
  - `challenges?select=title,entire_required,invite_jury_to_forks,chapter:chapters(name)`.
  - `app_settings`: keys only, never print values.
- **GitHub**, with the `ehl-gg` token:
  - `GET /rate_limit` (free);
  - `GET /orgs/european-hackathon-league/repos?type=all&per_page=100`
    (fork `created_at` + `description`);
  - `GET /repos/european-hackathon-league/<fork>/git/matching-refs/entire/checkpoints?per_page=100&page=N`;
  - `GET /repos/european-hackathon-league/<fork>/collaborators?affiliation=direct`
    and `/invitations`;
  - `GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/events` (MemberEvent = bot access time,
    kept for 90 days).
- **Actions logs:** `gh run list -R tum-ai/ehl --workflow process-code-reviews.yml`,
  then `gh run view <id> -R tum-ai/ehl --log | grep -E "Failed:|Completed\. Cost"`.
- **GitHub incidents:** `curl -s https://www.githubstatus.com/history.json?page=1`.
- **Ingest replay:** import `ingestRepo` from `@/lib/code-review/ingest` in
  an `.mts` file run by `node_modules/.bin/tsx` (top-level await needs ESM).
  Override `globalThis.fetch`:
  - pass through Supabase calls;
  - serve `/git/trees/` from the real API;
  - synthesize `/contents/` responses at the tree's byte sizes;
  - count the calls.

My top three solutions, ranked

1. Accept submissions immediately and process GitHub work through a durable queue.

Save the submission, its server receipt time and its processing job atomically. Return a receipt immediately. During a GitHub outage, classify remote verification as pending rather than rejecting an otherwise valid submission. Authentication, membership, required fields and deadline checks still apply.

A worker then verifies access, captures code and prepares jury access through resumable steps. It must respect retry headers, distinguish permanent permission failures from transient failures, and record diagnostic response details. Closing submissions and advancing the event must not wait for GitHub.

Use explicit states for verification, snapshot completeness and jury access. A nullable fork URL cannot represent all three.

Why first: This directly prevents GitHub failures from turning into lost submission opportunities.

Tradeoff: Receipt is provisional until remote requirements are verified. The interface and event rules must make that distinction clear.

2. Replace thousands of individual REST operations with bulk capture and reuse.

Fetch repository contents once for review, using a commit specific archive or Git checkout. Transfer Entire refs in batches through Git, including legacy checkpoint branches. Reuse the captured material for subsequent review attempts.

Where REST copying remains, use the SHA already returned by reference discovery and skip unchanged destination refs. Make checkpoint collection an explicit requirement rather than automatically doing it for every challenge. Archive API (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/contents#download-a-repository-archive-tar).

Why second: A queue alone makes excessive work orderly; it does not make that work affordable within the judging window.

Tradeoff: Bulk processing needs limits for repository size and transfer duration. Git operations also need pacing. A normal source archive does not contain all Git history or custom Entire refs.

3. Establish repository access early and provide an independent deadline fallback.

Verify private repository access and prepare jury permissions during the event, rather than doing everything at the deadline. Fix invitation pagination.

Define exactly which code version is submitted. Record an immutable commit identifier and preserve that version; do not later synchronize whatever happens to be on the default branch. If GitHub is unavailable, provide an authenticated code archive upload with a server receipt timestamp, including a checkpoint bundle where required.

Why third: A queue preserves the submission request, but cannot retrieve code while GitHub is unavailable. An independently received artifact also preserves what was submitted on time.

Tradeoff: This adds participant workflow and artifact handling. Without it, the event must explicitly accept delayed verification and the remaining uncertainty about deadline contents.

I recommend implementing solutions 1 and 2 together, with solution 3 as the outage contingency. The strongest objection is implementation scope, but merely increasing quota leaves verification failures, timeouts and stale snapshots unresolved. A second PAT belonging to the same user also shares that user’s quota; it is not independent capacity. GitHub authentication limits (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api).

Before declaring readiness, test 150 submissions with repeated updates, GitHub throttling, an outage, worker termination and more than 100 pending invitations. The acceptance criteria should include durable receipts, resumable processing and exact captured commit versions, not just successful HTTP responses.

content.text:
Overall, it's a good proposal and I agree with the ranking. It also caught two things my analysis missed. I checked those against the live data, and I'd push back on one part.

## Two points it caught that I missed, now confirmed

**1. "Record an exact commit" is a real gap.** No submission stores a commit SHA anywhere. The fork is synced to whatever is on the default branch *whenever the lock runs* (`merge-upstream` at `lib/github.ts:129`). On Zurich day, that captured different moments for different teams:
- **zurich-oasis**: submitted at 10:15:56, but the fork's latest commit is from **10:16:54**. A later lock pass pulled in code committed after the team submitted.
- **zurich-benevolent-agent-hive**: the team pushed again at **10:41**, but the fork stayed at 09:43. The lock never reached it.

So the jury saw code from inconsistent moments, and nothing records what was actually submitted. Commit timestamps can be set by the author, so these two are signs of the problem, not proof. I'd move this higher than the proposal's third item.

**2. Invite pagination is a real bug, but it can't hurt us today.** `acceptPendingInvite` only reads the first 100 pending invites (`lib/github.ts:73`). `ehl-gg` has **7** pending right now, so nothing breaks yet. It becomes a problem once more than 100 invites are pending, which a 150-team event could reach. It's a two-line fix.

## Where I agree without changes
- **Solution 1** is the core fix and matches my recommendation. Putting it before everything else is right.
- **Separate states** for verification, snapshot and jury access: yes. Today an empty `fork_url` can't tell "not tried yet", "GitHub down" and "team revoked access" apart.
- **"A second PAT from the same user shares the quota"**: correct, the limit is per account.
- **"A queue alone doesn't make the work affordable"**: correct. At the measured ~216 requests per Zurich-like team, a queue only turns failures into a long backlog.
- **Commit-specific archive for reviews**: one call instead of the median 198.
- **Test plan**: good, especially worker termination and more than 100 pending invites. It should run on a **separate test bot account**, not `ehl-gg`.

## Where I'd push back or add

**1. Solution 3's archive upload is expensive for a rare case. Recording the commit SHA gets most of its value almost for free.**
- A code archive won't fit through our platform: Vercel rejects request bodies over about 4.5 MB before our code runs (`CLAUDE.md`, Data Integrity 6). It would need direct browser-to-storage uploads, plus participants building git bundles.
- The cheaper alternative: have the team enter the **commit SHA** at submit, even when GitHub is down. A SHA is a fingerprint of the exact code. Once our server records it with a timestamp, the team can't swap the code later without the SHA changing. When GitHub is back, the worker fetches exactly that commit.
- That proves what was submitted on time with no upload. Keep the archive upload only as a last resort.

**2. "Treat verification as pending during an outage" needs an event rule before any code.**
Suppose a team's private repo still can't be opened after the deadline. How long do they get to fix access before the submission is invalid? The proposal names this trade-off but doesn't decide it. The organizers have to, because it decides disputes.

**3. The biggest win from solution 3 is doing the work early, not the fallback.**
Create the fork when a team **verifies** its repo during the hackathon, not at the deadline. Fork creation then spreads over hours. The deadline only has to record the SHA and sync once. That removes the "80 writes per minute" problem for 100+ teams better than any queue tuning.

**4. It leaves out a GitHub App, which does give separate capacity.**
The proposal is right that a second PAT doesn't help. A GitHub App installed on the snapshot org has **its own** request budget, separate from `ehl-gg`. It's worth considering for the worker. It doesn't help during an outage, though.

**5. It doesn't sequence the work, and the full build is big.**
If an event comes before all of this is built, a few small fixes remove most of the risk on their own:
- stop the review download loop when the budget is full;
- reuse the SHA from the ref list and skip refs that are already copied;
- only copy refs where Entire is required;
- set "pitching" without waiting for GitHub;
- fix invite pagination;
- log GitHub's error text and headers.

Each is a few hours of work, and together they target most of the failures we measured.

## What I'd do
1. **Small fixes first**, before the next event.
2. **Queue plus explicit states** (the proposal's solution 1), with the **commit SHA recorded at submit**.
3. **Create forks when a team verifies its repo**, and bulk git copying in a worker (its solution 2).
4. **Archive upload** only if the organizers decide an outage must never delay verification.

Should I add this review and the two new findings (the unpinned code versions and invite pagination) to `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`?

captures `API_URL` / `ANON_KEY` / `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` into `$GITHUB_ENV` as

(overriding the remote test secrets for that job) -> `pnpm test:seed-local` -> dev server ->
Playwright -> `supabase stop`.

> **Migration ordering note:** `supabase start` applies each migration file in its own
> transaction and in strict filename order. So (1) a freshly `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`'d
> enum value cannot be USED in the same file, and (2) no migration may forward-reference an
> object a later migration creates. See `CLAUDE.md` -> "E2E runs on an EPHEMERAL local
> Supabase" for the guard patterns.

The local changes are a well-built implementation of the handoff plan, and every check passes. But I wouldn't turn the feature on for an event yet: one missing setting stops the Actions worker from running at all, and the riskiest part (the git copy to GitHub) has never run against real GitHub.

## What the changes address

**Small fixes to the existing submission flow** (apply to every match right away):

| Handoff item | Change |
|---|---|
| D1, D2: wasteful ref copying | Reuses the commit SHA the ref list already returns; skips refs the fork already has |
| D3: copying where not needed | Refs are copied only when the challenge has `entire_required` (Zurich paid for about 770 refs without needing them) |
| Invite pagination | The bot's pending invites are read page by page (`lib/github.ts`) |
| Silent sync failures | A failed `merge-upstream` is now reported instead of ignored |
| E: review download bug | Once the reading budget is full, the review trims the last file and stops, instead of downloading and discarding the rest |

**The new "reliable submissions" mode.** It's switched on per chapter and off by default; migration 00071 adds it.
- **Submitting only saves to the database** (`receive_submission`), so GitHub being down no longer blocks a submission (the handoff's B).
- **Separate states** for verification, snapshot and jury access, plus a queue of jobs (prepare, observe, finalize) with leases, so a restarted worker can't overwrite newer work.
- **The deadline is closed inside the database**: locking and setting "pitching" no longer wait for GitHub (C).
- **An exact commit is frozen per repo**, fixing the unpinned-version problem.
- **Every GitHub response is logged** with its status, message and rate-limit headers (A), and one shared **request budget per GitHub account** paces all requests (at most 4 at once, 300 per minute, 20 writes per minute).
- **Git transfer** (option 4) runs in GitHub Actions, and **reviews download one archive per commit**.
- A new admin page for retry, approve and reject. Participants see their capture status on the form.

## Test results

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Typecheck | passes |
| Unit tests | **1,286 of 1,286 pass** (117 files, 24 new) |
| Production build | passes |
| All 71 migrations applied from scratch in strict order | **00071 applies cleanly** |
| E2E lifecycle | **66 of 66 pass**, including the 4 new reliable-submission tests |

I ran E2E on the local Supabase with every production key blanked, so nothing touched GitHub, SMTP or Redis.

The new E2E tests cover the database side well:
- a submission is saved while GitHub is unreachable;
- outsiders can't read the new tables or fake an observed commit;
- a crashed worker's job is taken over, and the old worker can no longer write;
- 150 saved submissions are all locked and frozen at the deadline;
- submitting after the deadline is refused.

**What they don't cover: nothing talks to real GitHub**, and the 150 submissions arrive one after another, not at the same time.

## Findings, most serious first

1. **The production worker can't start.** The new workflow reads `vars.GITHUB_ORG`, but the repo has no Actions variables at all. The worker would stop with "configuration missing" on every run, so no frozen code would be captured and no reviews queued. The test workflow also needs `TEST_GH_PAT` and `vars.TEST_GITHUB_ORG`, which don't exist either.

2. **Two different tokens do the work.** The cron checks repos with the Vercel token (`ehl-gg`, the account teams invite). The Actions worker creates forks and fetches private repos with `GH_PAT`, whose owner is still unconfirmed. If `GH_PAT` isn't `ehl-gg`, it can't read private repos. And **every git error is treated as temporary with no retry limit**, so those jobs retry forever and never reach organizer review.

3. **The git copy is untested against real GitHub.** It fetches only the frozen commit (`--depth=1`) and then pushes it to the fork. GitHub may refuse a push from such a partial copy. Because of point 2, a refusal would look like "retrying" forever rather than an error. It needs one run in a test org before any event.

4. **The frozen commit is the last one observed, not the state at the deadline.**
   - Repos are checked every 5 minutes, and every minute during the last 10. The form does warn that a last-second push may be missed.
   - The real problem is outages. In a Zurich-style outage (08:43–10:44), checks fail, so a team's frozen commit is from before the outage, or missing, which sends it to organizer review.
   - The design handles an outage by queuing manual review rather than capturing the code. Having teams **enter their commit SHA when submitting** would close that gap.

5. **The 100-ref limit will send heavy Entire users to review.** Zurich source repos had **155, 199 and 334** checkpoint refs. Anything over 100 is marked truncated and needs review, which would have been 3 of 20 Zurich teams. The limit existed to keep REST costs down; with git transfer it can be raised a lot.

6. **Jury invites will take hours at scale.** Each juror is invited to each fork separately (one write each), and the budget allows 300 writes per hour. 150 teams × 9 jurors = 1,350 invites, about **4.5 hours** minimum. A GitHub team with read access to all forks would need only 9 invites.

7. **Changing only the branch creates a whole new fork** (`submission-<id>-v2`) of the same repo. That isn't needed, since the fork doesn't depend on the branch. If GitHub returns the existing fork under its old name instead of creating a second one, the job waits for the new name forever. I haven't confirmed GitHub's behavior here.

8. **One admin won't see capture data.** Admins can read the new rows only if their profile's role is `admin`, but admin access is granted by email allowlist. In production, **1 of the 9 allowlisted admins who have a profile has role `participant`**. On pages that use the admin's own login, that admin would see no frozen repo links.

9. **Smaller issues:**
   - `CLAUDE.md` still says 70 migrations, and the new `lib/submission-processing/` folder isn't in its project-structure list. The repo rules require both.
   - The form checks capture status every 15 seconds even on matches without the new mode.
   - Normal "fork doesn't exist yet" 404s get logged as failures, which clutters the new error log.

## Housekeeping

- **The local database was rebuilt** to test the migrations, so its old test data (4 chapters, 8 submissions) is gone. A data backup is at `…/scratchpad/local-db-backup.sql`, which is deleted when this session ends.
- **I found a mistake in my own handoff numbers and corrected them in `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`.** GitHub's ref-list endpoint ignores paging and always returns the full list. My counting script therefore added the same 100 refs five times. The real totals are **Munich 1,322** refs, not ≥2,922, and **Zurich 770**, not ≥2,770. The capped forks hold 100 each, not 500+. My earlier claim that refs were copied "5+ times per fork" was wrong. The new code's assumption that this endpoint isn't paginated is **correct**.
- Nothing was committed, and the dev server is stopped.

To fix before this mode is used at an event:
1. Add the missing workflow variables and secrets (item 1).
2. Confirm who owns `GH_PAT` (item 2).
3. Do one real git-transfer run against a test org (item 3).
4. Raise the 100-ref limit (item 5).

Items 1 and 5 plus the doc updates are code or config changes I can make now. Items 2 and 3 need you or a test org.

# Review of submission capture hardening

The feature remains off by default. Code and workflow changes are local until reviewed and released. Production configuration has not been changed.

## Findings and disposition

1. **Worker configuration:** The repository currently has no Actions organization variables. However, the previous worker also read database settings, so missing variables alone did not prove startup failure. Its environment token override could select a different bot from cron. Both capture paths now use `github_token` and `github_org` from their database exclusively. The capture workflows no longer use `GH_PAT`, `TEST_GH_PAT` or Actions organization variables. Test database settings must identify a separate test bot and organization. The encrypted Actions secret's owner was not determined; the new capture worker no longer depends on that secret.

2. **Git transfer:** Full ancestry replaces depth one fetching. Authentication, permission and remote policy refusals go to organizer review immediately. Other transfer failures stop after five attempts; an explicit organizer retry resets that counter. Already verified captures can retry jury access without fetching from the original repository again. A local bare Git integration test is included, but it does not establish that GitHub accepts the operation for the intended organization. A real test organization rehearsal remains required.

3. **Cutoff policy:** The last platform observation before the deadline remains authoritative, as previously agreed. This can be old or absent during an outage. No newer commit is silently substituted. A participant supplied SHA could support a different policy, but does not itself prove repository access or code availability and would change the accepted cutoff rule. It is not introduced in this correction.

4. **Entire limit:** Reliable captures now retain up to 2,000 checkpoint refs. Tests cover 334 refs and the overflow case. The legacy REST copying cap remains 100 because that path still incurs per-ref API work. Git command timeouts and archive limits remain bounded; raising the ref cap does not guarantee that arbitrarily large repositories finish within the worker budget.

5. **Jury access:** The original 1,350 invitation calculation is valid for 150 forks and nine jurors, before counting fork creation or repeated stages. Completed individual invitations are now persisted across stages. An optional existing GitHub team can receive read access once per fork. This is roughly 150 repository grants plus membership setup, not only nine writes. Assigned jurors must have active team membership, and operators must check that the team contains only intended reviewers. No GitHub organization membership was changed.

6. **Branch changes:** Changing the branch invalidates observations while retaining the prepared fork and its jury grants. Changing the source repository clears them. Fork names depend on source repository identity rather than branch revision, and workers retain the actual repository returned by GitHub's fork response. Parent/source identity is still verified before using it.

7. **Admin reads:** Migration 00072 adds a restricted database helper for admin allowlist reads, including users with a stale profile role. It does not change application login guards or grant participant writes. The reported production count of affected admins was not independently queried.

8. **Smaller corrections:** Legacy matches no longer poll capture status. Expected destination 404/202 responses are suppressed in failure diagnostics. Both project instruction files describe 70 migration files through 00072 and the new source folder.

## Corrections to the review's scope claims

The shared limiter covers requests made through the new capture client. It does not cover every legacy GitHub caller. Diagnostics record failures, not every successful response. The 150 submission test is sequential, consistent with the expected event pattern; it is not a simultaneous load test. Historical incident totals in the handoff were not remeasured here. The implementation treats matching refs as one unpaginated response.

## Before an event

Apply both capture migrations. Configure the same shared bot settings for cron and Actions in the target database. Use different settings in the test database. Rehearse private source access, fork creation, full Git transfer, Entire refs, jury access and worker interruption against a test organization. Verify the resulting SHA in GitHub and the jury's access. Configure an existing jury team if the event's invitation volume requires it. Communicate the observed-commit cutoff rule before enabling the mode.

No database rebuild is required by migration 00072.

GitHub references: [fork creation and returned repository](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/forks#create-a-fork), [team repository permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/teams/teams#add-or-update-team-repository-permissions).

## Validation of this correction

Typecheck and production build passed. All 1,303 unit tests passed, including the local Git copy test. The full lifecycle suite passed all 68 tests against the dedicated test database. Migration 00072 was applied only there. Production GitHub permissions and a real GitHub transfer remain unverified. No project dependencies or commits were added.
